pure-polynucleotide-pdrn.summary: Salmon-derived DNA-fragment skin booster injected into the skin to improve texture, scars and fine lines by supporting tissue repair.

quick.overview:
PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide) is a mixture of DNA fragments, today mostly purified from salmon or trout, injected into the skin as a 'skin booster'. People use it for better skin texture, softer scars and fewer fine lines, often as an alternative or add-on to hyaluronic acid boosters.

The idea is that PDRN breaks down into components such as adenosine, which acts on the A2A receptor and is linked in lab work to blood-vessel growth and tissue-repair signalling, so skin quality and healing improve. Human trials so far mostly cover wounds, tendons and joints, with cosmetic scar and wrinkle trials registered but small and recent.
quick.how: It is a clinic procedure: a clinician places small deposits into the skin of the face or other areas, usually as a short series of sessions, and it is sometimes combined with other skin treatments. Users typically look for gradual changes in texture and healing over the weeks after sessions.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects in the trials surveyed are generally minor, and purified products are described as having low immunogenicity. Injection-site reactions and the usual risks of intradermal procedures apply. Regulatory status differs by country and product, being a medicine in some places and a device or cosmetic in others.

angle.text: PDRN is an injectable salmon-derived skin booster, borrowed from wound-care medicine, that people use for better skin texture, softer scars and fewer signs of aging. It works by supporting the skin's repair signalling so quality and healing improve. Human trials so far mostly cover wounds and tendons, with cosmetic studies still small.

volite-volift.summary: Low-concentration hyaluronic acid gel injected into the skin (not beneath it) to make it smoother and more hydrated rather than add volume.

quick.overview:
Juvéderm Volite (also sold as Skinvive, gel VYC-12) is a crosslinked hyaluronic acid gel placed in the skin to give smoother, more hydrated, finer-textured skin, particularly on the cheeks, without adding volume. Volift is a different product in the same family, a filler for lines and folds.

The hyaluronic acid binds water in the dermis, which is meant to improve surface smoothness and hydration, and it is described as lower-concentration and longer-lasting than older boosters. Published work includes a prospective single-arm study in people with cheek roughness, a retrospective cohort, a small randomised split-face trial with botulinum toxin and several manufacturer-sponsored trials.
quick.how: A clinician injects small amounts of gel into the dermis at multiple points across the cheeks or other areas. It is often paired with botulinum toxin or fillers as a skin-quality step, with results assessed over the following weeks.
quick.risks: Reported effects are mainly injection-site swelling, redness and bruising. Hyaluronic acid fillers carry rarer risks including lumps, delayed inflammatory reactions and vascular complications. It is a regulated device administered by clinicians.

angle.text: Juvéderm Volite (VYC-12, also sold as Skinvive) is injected into the skin to leave it smoother and more hydrated rather than to add volume. The hyaluronic acid binds water in the dermis, improving surface texture. Trials exist, mostly single-arm and manufacturer-linked.

restylane-vital-skinboosters.summary: Galderma's small-dose hyaluronic acid injections placed in the skin for better hydration, elasticity and smoothness; the longest-used skin booster.

quick.overview:
Restylane Vital is a stabilised hyaluronic acid gel (NASHA) from Galderma, injected as many tiny deposits in the skin to improve elasticity, hydration and smoothness rather than add volume. It sits at the centre of the 'skin booster' category, known in Korea as hydrofilling.

The hyaluronic acid binds water in the dermis, which leaves skin more hydrated and supple. Studies since 2008 have measured changes in elasticity and appearance on the face, neck, hands and elsewhere, including a 2010 pilot of 19 patients after three sessions, generally in small groups.
quick.how: A clinician places small amounts of gel in the mid-dermis using a needle, a cannula or a specialised injector, often in a short series of sessions. It is used on the face, neck and hands, and effects are described as temporary, so people repeat treatments.
quick.risks: Reported effects are usually temporary swelling, redness, bruising and small lumps. A case report describes persistent nodules on the neck after hyaluronic acid filler, and rarer risks include granulomas and vascular complications. It is performed by clinicians.

angle.text: Restylane Vital is the longest-used skin booster, with small hyaluronic acid deposits placed in the skin for smoother, more supple, hydrated skin. The gel binds water in the dermis, lifting elasticity and texture. Results come from small clinical studies and are described as temporary.

redensity.summary: Teoxane's Redensity hyaluronic acid gels smooth lip lines and soften under-eye hollows, with the change visible once placed.

quick.overview:
Redensity is the name Teoxane uses for several hyaluronic acid products. RHA Redensity is a 'resilient' filler for dynamic areas such as the lines around the mouth, and Teosyal PureSense Redensity 2 is used in the tear trough under the eyes to soften hollows.

The gel adds support and hydration where it is placed, so creases look smoother and the under-eye area looks less hollow. A randomised, evaluator-blinded multicenter study of RHA Redensity for moderate-to-severe perioral lines ran 52 weeks against a no-treatment control, and a prospective observational study looked at Redensity 2 around the eyes.
quick.how: A clinician injects the gel under or into the skin of the target area, often the perioral lines or tear trough, and the smoothing is visible right away. The RHA range is described as stretching and returning with facial movement, and treatments are repeated as the gel gradually breaks down.
quick.risks: Typical effects of hyaluronic acid fillers include swelling, bruising and lumps, with vascular and delayed inflammatory reactions rarer. Hyaluronic acid filler can be dissolved with hyaluronidase, and a 2023 study tested how 21 fillers respond to it.

angle.text: Teoxane's Redensity hyaluronic acid gels smooth lines around the mouth and soften under-eye hollows, with the change visible as soon as the gel is placed. A randomised 52-week trial studied RHA Redensity for perioral lines.

sunekos.summary: Italian injectable blending hyaluronic acid with amino acids as a 'biorevitalising' booster for firmer, less crepey face and body skin.

quick.overview:
Sunekos is an injectable that combines hyaluronic acid with amino acids, offered in clinics for photoaged face skin, the eye area and lax skin on the thighs, knees and arms. People use it for firmer, less crepey skin.

The idea is that the amino acids supply building blocks for collagen and elastin and support fibroblast activity, so skin tissue is stimulated. Published work includes a multicenter cellulite study of 46 women, and registered small studies cover the face, under-eyes and body.
quick.how: A clinician injects the mixture into or beneath the dermis at several points over the area being treated, typically across a short course of sessions. It is used on the face, around the eyes and on body skin.
quick.risks: The cellulite study assessed safety alongside efficacy. As with other injectables, local swelling and bruising are expected, and long-term safety data are limited.

angle.text: Sunekos is an Italian biorevitalising booster that combines hyaluronic acid and amino acids, used for firmer skin on photoaged faces, around the eyes and on lax areas like the thighs and arms. The amino acids are meant to supply building blocks for collagen and elastin. Support is mainly small manufacturer-linked trials.

exosome-facial.summary: Skin-quality treatment applying cell-derived vesicle products after microneedling or laser to improve texture and scarring; no exosome product is FDA-approved.

quick.overview:
An exosome facial applies or injects a product marketed as containing exosomes, tiny vesicles released by cells, usually after microneedling or laser. People use it for smoother texture, fewer acne scars and better overall skin quality, and it is positioned as a next step beyond PRP.

Exosomes carry RNA and proteins between cells, and proponents say products from stem-cell or other sources signal skin cells to repair tissue and lift skin quality. Most supporting research is cell and animal work, and registered human studies are small, mostly 7 to 40 people.
quick.how: A clinic applies the product to skin opened up by microneedling or laser, or injects it, as a single session or short series. Source cells named for these products include stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord and plants.
quick.risks: The FDA stated in 2019 that no exosome products were approved and reported serious adverse events in patients given unapproved exosome-labelled products in Nebraska. Product sources and quality vary between providers.

angle.text: Exosome facials apply a cell-derived product after microneedling or laser to improve skin texture, scarring and overall quality by boosting the skin's repair signals. Human studies so far are small and early, and no exosome product is FDA-approved.

mesogun.summary: Handheld multi-injector that places small intradermal doses of hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP across the face for hydration and glow.

quick.overview:
A mesogun is a handheld device that fires many tiny injections into the skin in quick succession. It is used in mesotherapy to deliver solutions such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP across the face for a hydrated, brighter-looking complexion.

A spring or pressure mechanism pushes a small amount of solution into the dermis with each press, so the active ingredients reach the skin without repeated manual injections. Device-specific research is limited to a lab delivery study on ink in foam and pig skin, a skin-hydration trial of a stamp-type injector and a few case reports.
quick.how: A clinic fills the device with the chosen solution and works across the face in a pattern of many shallow injections, often in a series of sessions. It is sometimes paired with PRP, and results are judged on glow and hydration over the following weeks.
quick.risks: Reported problems include a rosacea flare after a stamp-type microneedle injection and infection clusters after mesotherapy in Australia. Cosmetic mesotherapy has not been tested in standard clinical trials, and regulation of what gets injected varies by country.

angle.text: A mesogun delivers mesotherapy solutions such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP across the face through many tiny injections, aimed at a hydrated, brighter-looking skin glow. Research specific to the device is limited to a lab study, a hydration study and case reports.

prp-platelet-rich-plasma-injections.summary: Injectable made from your own concentrated blood platelets, used for skin rejuvenation, under-eye areas and hair; trials are mostly on knees.

quick.overview:
PRP is made by spinning your own blood to concentrate platelets, then injecting or applying it. In aesthetics it is used for fresher skin, fewer fine lines, brighter under-eyes and hair, and is often paired with microneedling as the 'vampire facial'. Under-eye hollows and dark circles are a common focus, often compared with hyaluronic acid tear-trough filler.

Platelets contain growth factors and cytokines thought to promote tissue repair, which is how treated skin is expected to look fresher. Most controlled trials are on knee osteoarthritis and other joint problems with mixed results, and facial studies are small case series.
quick.how: A blood draw is centrifuged in a clinic, and the plasma is injected with fine needles or mesotherapy devices, or applied after microneedling, usually as a short series of sessions. It is used on the face, under-eyes and scalp.
quick.risks: Adverse effects are low in most trials, but the CDC linked three HIV diagnoses in 2024 to an unlicensed spa reusing contaminated equipment for vampire facials. PRP itself is not FDA-regulated, so clinical use is off-label, while the preparation devices need clearance.

angle.text: PRP uses your own concentrated platelets, injected or applied with microneedling, for fresher skin, fewer fine lines and brighter under-eyes. The platelets' growth factors are thought to support tissue repair. Trial evidence is mostly from knee osteoarthritis rather than faces.

prf-platelet-rich-fibrin.summary: Fibrin-clot cousin of PRP from your own blood, standard in dental surgery and tried by forum users for dark under-eye circles.

quick.overview:
PRF is made by spinning your own blood without anticoagulant so platelets and white cells are trapped in a fibrin clot. Forum users on looksmax.org try it for dark under-eye circles and eye bags, hoping for a lighter, fuller eye area, and it also appears as a component of clinic-made or DIY facial serums.

Activated platelets in the fibrin matrix release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and EGF, which are thought to support tissue quality. It is established in dental and oral surgery for socket preservation, sinus lifts and periodontal regeneration, while the published trials are dental and none examine under-eye appearance. User reports on dark circles are mixed.
quick.how: Blood is drawn and centrifuged immediately in a clinic, and the resulting clot layer is used as a material or processed into a serum or injectable. For the eye area it is a clinic-made or DIY approach rather than a standard protocol.
quick.risks: No controlled safety data exist for under-eye injection or homemade serums in the sources reviewed. PRF preparation falls under an FDA product code that is 510(k) exempt.

angle.text: Forum users try PRF, a fibrin clot made from their own blood, for dark under-eye circles and eye bags, hoping growth factors lighten and fill the area; reports are mixed. It is established in dental surgery, and no facial trials were found.

liquid-facelift.summary: Filler-based facelift without surgery: injectables placed in several face areas in one session restore volume and contour for an immediately lifted look.

quick.overview:
A liquid facelift uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, in several facial areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The change is visible immediately, giving a lifted, more youthful face.

Fillers replace volume lost with aging in facial compartments. Most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months. The phrase is a marketing term, also used in a 2018 case series for a water-jet liposuction technique alongside surgical facelift; the literature is mostly narrative reviews.
quick.how: A clinician plans several injection areas, such as cheeks, temples, jawline and lines around the mouth, and places filler in one session. People repeat it as the filler gradually breaks down.
quick.risks: Common effects are bruising, redness and pain. Rare but serious risks include infection, lumps, vascular embolization and permanent vision loss. Fillers are FDA-regulated medical devices.

angle.text: A liquid facelift is the marketing term for placing fillers, often hyaluronic acid, in several face areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The lifted look is visible immediately and lasts around six months for most fillers.

collagen-induction-therapy.summary: Microneedling: controlled skin punctures that trigger collagen repair for smoother texture and softer acne and other scars.

quick.overview:
Collagen induction therapy, usually called microneedling or dermarolling, uses a roller, stamp or motorised pen with fine needles to puncture the skin many times. People use it for softer acne and other scars, stretch marks, fine lines, firmer skin and smoother texture.

The punctures create micro-channels and tiny injuries in the dermis, and the skin responds with a healing cascade of inflammation, fibroblast activity and new collagen over weeks to months, leaving the epidermis largely intact. Published studies, mostly small or retrospective, report improvement in scars and some photoaging, with larger controlled evidence more limited.
quick.how: It is done in clinics with professional devices or at home with rollers and pens, typically as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. It is often combined with PRP or topical products, and results build gradually over months.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary irritation. Infections, pigment changes and scarring appear in complication reviews, and public-health authorities have warned of blood-borne infection when needling is paired with blood-derived products in unregulated settings. Professional devices are regulated as medical devices in the US, while home devices vary widely.

angle.text: Microneedling punctures the skin with fine needles so it repairs itself and builds new collagen, aimed at softer scars, smoother texture and fewer fine lines. Scars are the best-studied use, with more modest evidence for wrinkles and texture.

aqualyx.summary: Deoxycholate injectable sold in Europe to dissolve small pockets of fat; forum users use it to slim the jaw, cheeks and neck.

quick.overview:
Aqualyx is a CE-marked injectable made from deoxycholic acid, a bile acid that dissolves fat cell membranes. In Europe it is sold to trained practitioners to reduce small fat pockets such as under the chin, and forum users discuss it for slimming the cheeks, jaw and neck to get a leaner, more defined lower face.

Deoxycholate acts like a detergent on fat cell membranes, the cells break open and the body clears the debris, with inflammation and later fibrosis described in the treated area. Published evidence is limited to small studies and case reports, and no published trial has tested facial hollowing as described in forums. The related drug Kybella is the US-approved deoxycholic acid product for submental fat.
quick.how: Practitioners inject it into the targeted fat pocket, sometimes with ultrasound guidance, over a series of sessions. Forum users report using it on the lower face, and claims of permanence are anecdotal.
quick.risks: Reported effects are swelling, bruising and pain, and a published case described chronic infection and nodule formation after a deoxycholate injection. Aqualyx is not FDA-approved, counterfeits have been discussed in forums, the manufacturer sells only to trained professionals and self-injection is outside labelled use.

angle.text: Aqualyx is a deoxycholate injectable sold in Europe to dissolve localized fat, and forum users discuss it for slimming the cheeks, jaw and neck. It breaks down fat cells in the treated area so the lower face looks leaner. Facial use goes beyond published studies, and claims of permanence are anecdotal.

follicular-unit-extraction-fue.summary: Hair transplant that removes follicles one by one from the back of the scalp and implants them in thinning areas, without a linear scar.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit extraction is a hair transplant technique in which small circular punches remove individual follicular units, usually one to four hairs, from the back and sides of the scalp and implant them in thinning or bald areas. The payoff is a fuller hairline and denser coverage once grafts grow in, without the linear scar of strip harvesting.

Grafts from the donor zone keep their resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hair is described as long-lasting. The technique was introduced in the early 2000s as an alternative to strip harvesting (FUT), leaving tiny scattered scars instead, though drawbacks include longer surgery, higher cost and a steep learning curve for surgeons.
quick.how: Surgery is done under local anaesthetic, with grafts extracted using punches of about 0.6 to 1.0 mm and placed into small recipient incisions. Robotic systems exist to assist, and variants include sapphire FUE and DHI. Transplanted hair grows in over the following months.
quick.risks: Described effects include temporary swelling, shock loss of transplanted hair, folliculitis, numbness, transected follicles and, rarely, scarring. Over-harvesting can leave a thinned donor area, and native hair loss can continue after surgery, sometimes needing further procedures. Results depend on the surgeon.

angle.text: FUE is a hair transplant method that moves follicles one by one from the donor scalp to receding or thinning areas, building a fuller hairline without a linear donor scar. The new hair is visible once grafts grow in, at the cost of longer surgery.

follicular-unit-transplantation-fut.summary: Strip-harvest hair transplant: a scalp strip is dissected into grafts and moved to thinning areas, leaving a thin linear donor scar.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit transplantation removes a thin strip of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which technicians dissect under microscopes into natural follicular units and implant in balding areas. The payoff is visible new density in thinning areas.

Grafts from the donor zone retain resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hairs are described as lasting. It became the standard hair transplant approach in the 1990s and allows many grafts from a single session, and it is often compared with follicular unit extraction (FUE), which avoids a strip incision.
quick.how: The strip is taken under local anaesthetic, the wound is closed with sutures, and technicians prepare the grafts for implantation. Recovery includes stitches or staples and about two weeks of healing, with transplanted hair growing in over the following months.
quick.risks: The donor site keeps a thin linear scar, usually hidden by surrounding hair. Shock loss and other graft-related effects are described, along with the general risks of surgery.

angle.text: FUT, or strip harvesting, moves hair from a strip of donor scalp to thinning areas, giving visibly denser hair at the cost of a thin linear donor scar usually hidden by hair. It is the older of the two main harvest methods.

direct-hair-implantation-dhi.summary: FUE hair transplant variant that places grafts with a pen-style implanter, promoted for precise angle and density at the hairline.

quick.overview:
Direct hair implantation uses a hollow pen-like implanter, the Choi pen, to place extracted follicular units straight into the scalp without pre-cut recipient slits. Clinics say it gives control over angle and direction, which suits delicate areas like the hairline, for a denser hairline and crown.

Follicles are extracted as in FUE, loaded into the implanter and inserted in a single step. Grokipedia reports longer procedures, higher skill needs, fewer grafts per session and costs around 40 to 60 percent above standard FUE; no controlled comparison with other methods was found.
quick.how: Extraction is done as in FUE under local anaesthetic, then each graft is loaded into the pen and implanted in one step. Sessions are slower than standard FUE.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE generally, including swelling, folliculitis and follicle transection. Cost is higher and sessions typically cover fewer grafts.

angle.text: DHI is an FUE variant that uses an implanter pen to place grafts in one step, promoted by clinics for precise angle and density, especially at the hairline. The transplanted hair is visible as it grows in; independent comparisons with other methods are scarce.

sapphire-fue.summary: FUE hair transplant variant using sapphire blades for recipient incisions, promoted for finer channels, denser placement and quicker healing.

quick.overview:
Sapphire FUE is a hair transplant in which the recipient channels are cut with sapphire blades rather than steel. Clinics describe finer incisions, about 0.5 to 1.0 mm, that may allow denser placement, less bleeding, faster healing and less visible scarring for a denser hairline.

Follicles are extracted as in standard FUE, then implanted into the channels. Evidence comparing blade types is limited: a 2026 paper compared sapphire and steel blades, and a registered trial studied a topical agent for wound healing after sapphire FUE.
quick.how: It follows the standard FUE routine under local anaesthetic, with sapphire-tipped blades used to make the recipient sites before grafts are placed. Hair grows in over the following months.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE in general, such as swelling, shock loss and folliculitis.

angle.text: Sapphire FUE is promoted as giving hair transplants finer incisions, denser graft placement and faster healing, for a fuller hairline with less visible scarring. The restored hair is visible once it grows in, while comparisons of blade types are limited.

choi-implanter-pen.summary: Pen-style implanter that opens each recipient site and places the graft in one step; the tool behind DHI hair transplants.

quick.overview:
The Choi implanter pen is a hand-held tool used in some hair transplants to open the recipient site and insert a follicular unit in one step. It is the basis of the technique marketed as DHI, aimed at fuller hair in thinning areas.

Clinics say it gives control of the angle, direction and depth of each graft and shortens the time grafts spend outside the body. Reference sources note higher cost, longer procedures and fewer grafts per session, and no controlled trial comparing the pen with other placement methods was found.
quick.how: Follicular units are extracted individually as in FUE, loaded into the hollow pen and implanted directly without pre-made slits. Results depend heavily on the surgeon.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE hair transplantation generally, such as swelling, folliculitis, scarring and poor graft take.

angle.text: The Choi implanter pen is the tool behind DHI, placing each follicular unit in a single step to fill in thinning areas with control over angle and depth. Clinics promote its precision, and published comparisons with other methods are absent.

scalp-reduction.summary: Surgery that removes a section of bald scalp and pulls hair-bearing skin together to shrink the bald area visibly.

quick.overview:
Scalp reduction cuts out a segment of bald scalp and stitches hair-bearing skin together, so the bald area is smaller and surrounding hair covers more of the head. It has been described in surgical journals since at least 1980, often as an adjunct to hair transplants.

Published work consists of technique papers and case reports, including serial reductions analysed biomechanically, scalp extension techniques and a device for managing suture tension during closure; no trials were found.
quick.how: Bald skin is excised under surgery, and neighbouring scalp is advanced and sutured. Stretching techniques and serial procedures have been described, and it has been used alongside hair transplantation.
quick.risks: It is a surgical procedure with the usual risks of excision and closure, such as scarring. The sources reviewed do not give complication rates.

angle.text: Scalp reduction removes a segment of hairless scalp and pulls hair-bearing skin together, visibly shrinking the bald area so existing hair covers more of the head. It is an older adjunct to hair transplantation, described mainly in technique papers.

artas-robotic-system.summary: FDA-cleared image-guided robot that harvests donor hairs for FUE transplants, automating extraction to restore density in thinning areas.

quick.overview:
ARTAS is a robot from Restoration Robotics that finds and extracts donor hair follicles during FUE hair transplants, which restore density to the hairline and crown. It was reported cleared by the FDA in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with androgenetic alopecia.

Imaging maps the donor scalp and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units. It automates harvesting only, and implantation still involves the surgical team. Registered manufacturer-associated trials compare it with manual harvest, but no results were available in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: The surgical team uses the robot for the extraction step of an FUE session, then implants the grafts. Operators need training, and it is offered by clinics that own the system.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE generally. Reference sources note higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators.

angle.text: ARTAS is an FDA-cleared image-guided robot that automates donor hair extraction in FUE transplants, which restore visible density to the hairline and crown. Published outcome data comparing it with manual harvest are thin.

neograft.summary: Automated suction-assisted FUE device, reported FDA-approved in 2009, that extracts and delivers grafts for hair transplants.

quick.overview:
NeoGraft is a machine that automates part of FUE hair transplant harvesting, used to fill thinning areas for fuller coverage. Wikipedia describes it as the first robotic surgical device FDA-approved for hair restoration, in 2009.

Grokipedia describes it as using pneumatic pressure to extract and deliver grafts without twisting or pulling. Little outcome data has been published, and no comparison with other harvesting methods was identified.
quick.how: Follicular units are extracted from the donor scalp by pneumatic suction-assisted extraction, then implanted in thinning areas as in FUE.
quick.risks: Risks match FUE generally. A surgeon abstract presented in 2014 argued that most hair-restoration patients are not appropriate FUE candidates, whether extraction is manual or with NeoGraft or ARTAS.

angle.text: NeoGraft is an automated suction-assisted FUE device, reported FDA-approved in 2009, used to harvest and deliver grafts for hair transplants that restore coverage. Little outcome data has been published.
